Title: blah blah blah...our metagame this...our metagame that...

Messages.Author: kevin scribner
Messages.Body:
hey --

that statement really got under SOMEBODY'S skin... let's take a look
at it, shall we...?

first of all, i'm an american, and i don't get out of the country
much... if that limits my "meta-game," so be it...

but i play sanctioned tournaments in 3 venues on a regular basis: our
boston group, which now usually holds tourneys in waltham, which
introduces another element to "the metagame;" seekonk, a pricedom
encompassing southern massachusetts and much of rhode island; and
springfield, a third princedom covering the western part of the
state... all three areas are different, and each one is different
each time i go there... i don't play the same decks all the time, and
neither do the folks i play against... with a few exceptions, we're
all watching each others' first vampire with great interest...

in addition, at the northeast regional qualifier, i had the fantastic
opportunity to play with some of the greatest names in this game [not
including the greats i get to play with every week or every month:
peal, swainbank, hirsch, williams, garvin, jenner, and a host of
others], from all over the country: the tatus, kristoff, duffin,
steele, watkins, bakija, bresnehan, and more... representing atlanta,
columbus, detroit, new york, lansing [hi, bernie!], washington dc, and
other areas... the american metagame, i guess... but there's no such
thing...

so i don't think my deck building approach suffers from myopia -- i'll
go one step further: i don't take "metagame" considerations into
account when building decks, at least not specific ones... i try to
take into account the realities of the v:tes environment in general,
instead... and i like to think that any of my decks can survive a
transplanting into any environment as a result...

i guess i'm trying to point out the existence of a sort of
"uber-metagame" concept...

here's an example:

"ventrue law firm" -- classic deck archetype... but it sucks ass,
can't win... why...? because anyone who can't muster up a single
point of static intercept dosn't deserve a seat at a tourney table...
that's not a metagame issue, that's a gaping flaw in the deck: if
stopping your actions shuts you down, then someone will, and you will
lose... end of story...

does this make the usa better than england [or europe in general]...?
of course not... but nobody here tries to play that thing here
anymore, because it doesn't work... that's not a metagame issue --
it's facing the facts...

if it were a metagame issue, after a while, when someone poppped it as
a surprise, it'd wreak havoc all over the place -- but that's not
what's going to happen... it's just gonna fizzle, because it has no
way of making things happen...

which is why stealth vote is coming into favor... which is why you're
seeing on point of static intercept becoming two as a requirement...
and which is why draba is such a strong card... and blah blah blah...

and you can't say that the american metagame has evolved the need for
a point of static intercept -- the GAME itself has done that... there
are a stupid number of cards that are +1 stealth actions: if you like
taking them up the hole, then don't be able to block them... your
choice... and when jost, rebekka, muaziz, lucretia, or spider killer
hit the table, drop 'em, grab yer ankles, and start singing "moon
river" [with an assamite accent]...

mind you, that's just one example of a larger issue...

back to my play habits: i play in those three spots, mostly, and i
did pretty well at the qualifier, which had no metagame [not one you
could plan for, anyway]... i think it's important to build decks
regardless of local considerations, decks that can stand up
anywhere... i know that whatever i bust out at gencon is going to be
something that i think can withstand almost anything...

and i'm not talking about toolbox decks, though you have to address
unexpected develeopments... i'm all for toolboxes, especially at the
beginning of your "career," but that's not exactly what i'm trying to
sell here...

like this: 5 players sit down at a "torunament strength" table... it
turns out your grand prey actually brought a really bad,
casual-strength-at-best deck to the table... how does your deck
respond to this...? that's not a metagame issue -- it's a game
issue...

i don't think i'm making my point very well, so i'll cut it here and
let some better minds run with the ball for a while, see what bubbles
to the surface...

--khs

looking for a betta meta

Putting in intercept weakens the foundation of your deck, as it adds more
moving parts which get in the way. Sure, it isn't that difficult to get,
like, a single KRC in your deck, but having 1 intercept location does not
intercept equate, and without untap available, it is much less effective as
a defense--thus you start putting in untap and more intercept locations,
making the Rush aspect of the deck more dilute and less effective.

The Rush deck is all about drawing the hard line.

> point of my deck. Indeed. But if your prey has any common sense at all, he

> find a way to put some in there.

I disagree completely. And I succeed in many things past casual play.

Putting 1 card that provides permanent intercept in a deck is not adding
intercept defense. It is adding a lark card that might, once and a while,
possibly be useful, but more often than not will either never come up or
when it does not actually be useful (what is the pointof having a single KRC
when your predator is a deck with reliable +2 intercept?).

Putting 2 cards in that provide permanent intercept is leaving the deck in
the same place, only slightly less so.

Putting 4 cards in is starting to build a deck with reliable light
intercept, but also starting to compromise the main focus of the deck.

Sure, putting in 1 prayer card isn't going to hurt the deck, but it is going
to be just that--a prayer card. Sometimes it will help out, but most of the
time it won't come up or make a difference. I could put a single intercept
card in my Rush deck, but it wouldn't be as effective as any other prayer
card that I have tried out. Heck, right now my single prayer card is a
stinking Hell Hound, as I am more concerend about weenie horde bleeds than
+1 stealth.

> And I don't get the room/ability point. I'm sure everyone has heard of
> KRCG, London Evening Star and the Rumor Mill. For a measly 1 pool you have
> permanent intercept for as long as someone doesn't contest with you.

Again, 1 intercept location isn't going to help you. It is a lark.

>What kind of decks are we building that we cant afford an expenditure of one
> pool?

It isn't the expenditure of the 1 pool (or 2 or 3). It is that the single
card isn't, in most cases, going to make a difference. It isn't worth paying
2 or 3 pool for a card that isn't going to be that useful most of the time,
especially when the Master slot could be spent on something tha you *know*
will be useful (like Fame or hand cycling).

>You do have Tastes and Blood Dolls in your Weenie Potence Deck don't
> you? Is your Weenie Potence deck so master heavy with Potence Skill Cards
> that you can't afford to squeeze in one of the intercept locations?

Again, squeezing one in isn't the point. I could include one without much
effort. On the other hand, would doing so:

-Be particularly useful on a regular basis?
-Be worth spending the pool on?
-Be better than another Master card that I know will always be useful?

In the end, the answers to these questions in the context of my Rush deck is
no. And my rush deck does just fine without the +1 intercept.

I have other decks that use intercept, 'cause they need it and can use it
well. The Rush deck, however, doesn't really need it, and couldn't use it
that well anyway, so why include it?

Beginning? I find toolbox requires a lot more thought and experience to get to
work.

In the thread that produced this one, the defense module thread, someone
mentioned about taking a look at the top decks (of some major or something,
whatever they were from isn't the point) and saying to oneself "how did these
decks win?". Discussing that *is* the epitome of CCG analysis.

What wins? Why? How do you beat what wins? These are the essential questions
to analyzing games.

Hmmm, that's all very interesting, and i feel that as a VTES tourist i
should have something awfully profound to say about it, but i don't.
All i can do is offer some observations based on what has happened to
me when i've gone abroad and played good foreign players, plus some
impressions of what has happened to good foreign players when they
have come here.

i've played with quite a lot of the good E seaboard US players in the
USA, and in general i find that my good decks do ok against them
[though tweaking for the local play-style WAS beneficial]. Maybe they
were pulling their punches a bit, but i don't think so, not ALL the
time anyway. i've had a LOT of trouble trying to play American decks
in the UK [but see comments on Rehlow's Baron deck, below], though i
have to admit that one of my two constructed-deck tourney wins was
with a slightly-tweaked version of one of David Zopf's decks. Possibly
the moral of all that is that there isn't a PROFOUND difference
between the metagames or player abilities either side of the pond.

i actually met Ben Swainbank at the 2001 Euros where he did OK and i
did ABYSMALLY BADLY, partly because i lost my temper, but mainly
because my deck sucked donkey. And yet it didn't do so GLOBALLY,
because i swept up all the UK contingent with it on the boat going
over, and we all thought it was going to STORM into the finals in
Paris. But as it turned out, it wasn't focussed enough for the games
in which it actually played - ie this was a deck that was tuned for
the UK metagame, and it didn't work once outside our Sceptr'd Isle.
One of the other UK players [Barney Baker] got to the final there as
top seed, so once again we are not looking at big differences in
player ability but perhaps, this time, we DO have evidence of a
metagame difference between Europe and the UK. As further evidence of
that i played in the sealed-deck LOSERS tourney whilst the finals were
going on in Paris and i got to the final of that [Hi, 2nis! Hi Klav!]
but, sadly, had to leave before playing in it or miss my boat.

The previous year i had the pleasure of playing in the Lisbon tourney
and i got to the final there and shoulda won, really, but i took a
STUPID decision about seating and got weenie dominate-swarmed. Again,
evidence that the metagame and player abilities are less different
than you might think, either side of the Bay of biscay.

i've been lucky enough to entertain a number of good American players
at Legbiter Hall and to play both casual and competitive games with
them, with ROUGHLY even honours all round. i feel i have to single out
SSgt Michael Eichler here as AFAIK the ONLY foreign player who has
come to a UK tourney and actually WON; he did this essentially by
playing his own game and keeping his head down in the face of UK-style
agitation IIRC, but perhaps his personal reflections would be useful
here. Off-topic Michael, if you are reading this, can you get Beef
Jerky off whatever the USAAF equivalent of the NAAFI is? If so, can
you lay by a store for me?

Finally at least in terms of factual stuff, one of my favourite decks
right now is Rehlow's Baron deck tweaked for the UK metagame. This is
an American deck and in its original form it was a trick-deck and
UTTERLY HOPELESS against good UK players fielding proper decks. But
the concept is sound, because now [after tweaking] i can sweep up
tables of good players with it, both here and the other side of the
channel. Contrary to what you might think, the key to making Rehlow's
idea work in Europe was FOCUSSING the deck, NOT toolboxing it, and i
actually used a pair of techniques which were invented by the American
players David Tatu ["Tatuisation"] and Ethan Burrow ["Modules"] to
help me do this.

i want to finish off by saying something about the issue which started
all this name-calling, ie Hunting Grounds and whether putting them
into your deck or not is a metagame issue. My view is that it is not a
metagame issue, but rather a ferocity issue. i am not ideologically
opposed to HGs and most of my decks contain one. However, of the four
decks i would currently pick from if my life depended on winning the
next game of Jyhad, NOT ONE contains even a SNIFF of a hunting-ground.
Why? Simply put, there are more powerful Master cards [including SR]
occupying their slot. So i think the nub of the difference between, on
the one hand Matt and Tony, and on the other Ben and Kevin, is that
Matt and Tony and i rate the OFFENSIVE potential of Master cards/slots
higher than the Newer Englishmen do. As evidence for this view,
consider Kevin's comment about the Ventrue Law Firm deck being hosed
by blocking. Not in its UK form it isn't, Kev - it'll be Arika or
Queen Anne or Suhailah who is calling the Parity shift [and/or they'll
be doing it in daylight], and what will be killing you isn't primarily
the votes anyway, but rather the takeover cards, and the fact that
you've already spent too much pool because the deck has just been
hanging around apparently-innoccuously until its hand has been built
for the killer blow.

Well, i hope some of this helps. Ah, soddit, all this being reasonable
is too much for me. Tony, Kev called your pint a limp-wristed Limey
Fag, he did too, i heard him. Kev, Tony wipes his bottom on the

Some things I've noticed within the US:

The Northeast Regionals, while won by Peter Bakija, were largely
dominated by the New Englanders. 7 of the top ten were from New
England. Nobody from the DC, Michigan, or Ohio groups qualified.

At the North Central Regionals, 6 of the top 11 were from Michigan,
and 4 were from Ohio (including the winner).

We haven't yet seen the tournament report, but the Mid-Atlantic
Qualifier, at least three from DC qualified, along with 2 from
New England. I got smacked around a bit, but I was also trying
out this 5-discipline Ravnos deck, so I probably deserved it. :)

So, my rough estimation is that despite the fair amount of cross-
pollination among American players, each group still has a definable
metagame of its own, and one will tend to do better within their
local metagame. At the same time, it kinda makes sense that at a
qualifier in New England, a lot of people from New England are going
to be there, and a lot of them may qualify. Same for DC players at
a DC qualifier, and Michigan players at a Michigan qualifier.

I don't think that's necessarily the case. I think it's more the case
that here in New England we look at cards in terms of their short-term,
medium-term, and long-term application and potential. We feel that a
Hunting Ground is a very powerful long-term card, and that we've seen
enough games go to a long-term situation that it's typically worth putting
one in a deck. A deck from New England will typically contain a Hunting
Ground and 3-4 Sudden Reversals (which are primarily used for the offensive
purpose of negating Blood Dolls and Minion Taps - though not exclusively
so). Ben Swainbank is weird and doesn't play with either Hunting Grounds
or Sudden Reversals, and yet still has a lot of success.

In some decks, I think Hunting Grounds can actually be considered to be
part of the decks' offensive infrastructure. Intercept-combat decks over
here tend to use Hunting Grounds, the Rack, P-base Montreal, Blood Dolls,
and so on as part of an infrastructure that gradually builds more and more
minions, while the intercept-combat part of the deck fends off assailants.

Perhaps a more accurate take on it is that English players place a stronger
emphasis on transient effects? *shrug*

That's nice in theory, but you can't "jam" the best interceptors. The
master locations are just playable. Contested, maybe. But you aren't
going to jam someone on them. Similarly, Winthrop, Raven Spy, and
Sport Bike just get deployed. 2nd trad is usable if you're tapped but
don't need the intercept yet. Ditto for read the winds, speak with
spirits. You'll want transients as well as those if you're playing
dedicated intercept but you don't need a ton even if you are.

can't get weapons other than GoB or DW. You can't get retainers and
allies. You can't vote. You can't 3rd, 4th, or 5th trad, nor can you
GtU @ superior. You can't rescue from torpor, you can't leave torpor.
You can't get equipment. List goes on and on. You can do rush
combat or bruise and bleed, but I'd hardly call those an auto-win no
matter what the environment.

> Besides, some decks just don't have the room/ability to use intercept. And
> some decks just don't need it (classic example: weenie potence rush) so why
> bother?

Usually so that you aren't giving up GW/VP to things that would
otherwise be stopped, as well as to create critical points for
yourself. I agree that weenies in general don't need it. They don't
want to block a lot. But they'll play delaying tactics or deflection
at times, as well as some wakes.

But (IMO) it's less often that there's a minion card worth paying
a pool and a master-phase action to cancel. Conditioning is
generally worth it. Govern is generally not. Immortal Grapple
is worth a shot but will often fail; Undead Strength there's not
even any point. Disarm would be worth doing. But there's too
much redundancy and too much ability to do something else bad
with the minion (again IMO) for DI to be worth its slot as often
as SR is. Master cards really do have "bigger swing effects"
more often; Minion Tap, Hostile Takeover, Temptation of Greater
Power, Fame, especially.

> Granted, master
> card plays tend to be (or should be) prominent events in the game, but so
> is "take six to the dome" and "I rip that guy's head off."

In other words, in my experience, you can rarely avoid taking
six to the dome, or having your head ripped off, with DI. You
might delay it a turn. You might not. Most of the time it
wasn't worth a pool and a master card slot and a master phase
action. At least, for me. This is probably in part due to my
feeling that most minion-card stuff people will do to you, you
need to have some minion-card plan of your own for dealing with
anyway, whether or not you're playing with DI. So it seems
"less worth it" to put in DIs as well, for when your plan fails
or DI will supplement it effectively.

Josh

See, this is where you're really getting to the point:
metagames evolve in response to what would be good in any
particular metagame, and then evolve in response to the
decks trying to take advantage of that, and so on. It's
not exactly circular, but it is a continuous process, and
any area that's at a different place than yours will have
different results (and opinions on "what's good").

There are certainly some deck types and strategies that are
more inter-metagame robust than others, and these are what
I think you're defining as "good stuff". But even these
can be vulnerable to having the metagame shift against them
at some point, as a result of new cards being printed, or
just a general shift in playstyle/strategies.

> and you can't say that the american metagame has evolved the need for
> a point of static intercept -- the GAME itself has done that... there
> are a stupid number of cards that are +1 stealth actions: if you like
> taking them up the hole, then don't be able to block them...

I agree to a large extent, but at the same time, you're
pointing at something else important by saying the GAME has
evolved the need for a point of intercept: the game (cards
available etc) *does* influence the metagame (what people
actually play) and if there are a lot of strong +1 stealth
actions then having +1 intercept becomes more valuable.

Anyway, just some thoughts on the issue.

Josh
